problems.description: app.py defines a class in snake_case instead of PascalCase (per SonarQube/convention scan).
test_notification_server.py defines a class in snake_case instead of PascalCase (per convention scan).
test_notification_server.py has a module-level constant in lowercase instead of UPPER_CASE (per convention scan).

ClientRegistry wraps access in a threading.Lock although the server is fully asyncio single-threaded; harmless but unnecessary defensive overhead, and the registry dict is untyped (dict[str, WebSocketServerProtocol] would be clearer).
Imports WebSocketServerProtocol from websockets.legacy.server — a legacy module path; prefer the modern API to avoid deprecation churn in future websockets versions.

strengths: Clean protocol design with explicit message-type validation and a dedicated ProtocolError for malformed input.
Good separation of concerns: parse_message (protocol), ClientRegistry (state), NotificationServer (transport/dispatch).
Correct lifecycle handling — registration, welcome/join/leave broadcasts, and guaranteed unregister in finally.
Health endpoint served on the same port via process_request without extra machinery.
Comprehensive test suite (~272 lines) and clear docstrings with type hints throughout.
commit_reviews.summary: Well-architected greenfield notification server that follows existing patterns and ships with solid tests; the only blemishes are three minor convention violations flagged by the static scan and a few defensible-but-unnecessary design choices (threading lock in asyncio, legacy websockets import).

problems.description: Measurement flags 3 convention violations (score 0.83): PascalCase class names in test_notification_server.py (x2) and app.py. The app.py violation is outside this diff and pre-existing; the test-file ones fall in/around the added test block and are not addressed by the commit.
broadcast_to_channel awaits each subscriber send sequentially inside a loop (mirrors the existing broadcast pattern); at scale this serializes delivery to large channels and could use asyncio.gather.
ChannelRegistry._channels is an untyped dict (matching ClientRegistry's untyped style); type parameters like dict[str, set[str]] would aid clarity without breaking the pattern.
Channel names are validated only as non-empty strings — no length/format bounds, so clients can create arbitrary channel keys and grow the registry unboundedly.

strengths: ChannelRegistry cleanly mirrors the existing ClientRegistry pattern (dataclass + threading.Lock), so the feature slots into the established architecture rather than inventing a new mechanism
Subscription cleanup is wired into the connection teardown finally block via unsubscribe_all, preventing leaked subscriptions on disconnect
New /channels and /channels/{name}/subscribers HTTP endpoints follow the existing single-port interception pattern in _handle_http, with proper URL-decoding (unquote) and sorted output
subscribe/unsubscribe dispatch extends the existing if/elif message-type chain and returns explicit system error messages for malformed payloads
Comprehensive tests added for the new subscription paths
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, pattern-consistent feature addition — the channel registry reuses the ClientRegistry design, integrates with existing dispatch and HTTP handling, and ships with tests — mildly held back only by pre-existing/unaddressed naming-convention violations and an untyped dict field.

problems.description: Measured convention score is 0.83 with 3 flagged violations, but all three (app.py PascalCase; test_notification_server.py PascalCase + UPPER_CASE constants) live in files this single-file commit (+1 files) does not touch — they predate the diff rather than being introduced here.

Channel membership now exists as two sources of truth (in-memory ChannelRegistry plus the Redis mirror in RedisConnectionState); correctness depends on careful reconnect reconciliation, and the truncated diff leaves that re-sync path (and worker-task lifecycle on start/stop) unverifiable.

Adds a hard runtime dependency on redis.asyncio and a broker (localhost:6379) to the core server; the visible diff shows defaults but no explicit graceful-degradation path for a Redis outage on publish.

strengths: Faithfully implements the Session 3 spec: Redis pub/sub backbone, Redis-mirrored connection state, SQLite history, GET /messages with limit/offset, and REDIS_URL/DATABASE_URL env config.
Clean single-purpose abstractions — RedisConnectionState and MessageStore isolate each new backing store.
Centralized Redis key-naming helpers (redis_channel_key, redis_direct_key, etc.) keep the key scheme consistent.
Defensive query-param parsing via _parse_int for the new endpoint.
Extends existing patterns (ClientRegistry.channels_of, updated module docstring) without breaking prior functionality.
commit_reviews.summary: A faithful, well-decomposed integration session that lands the required Redis pub/sub backbone, Redis-mirrored connection state, and SQLite persistence cleanly while preserving prior behavior — with the only measured convention hits sitting in files outside this commit's diff.

problems.description: Speculative generality (YAGNI): the new BaseTransport abstraction (+~150 lines, 2 new classes) has only one concrete implementation (WebSocketTransport). The SSE/long-polling/TCP transports are hypothetical, so the added surface has no immediate consumer beyond a single subclass.

Type safety regression in ClientRegistry: add/get were loosened from WebSocketServerProtocol to Any, and TRANSPORT_REGISTRY is an untyped dict. These could be typed as Dict[str, Type[BaseTransport]] and a Protocol/type-parameterized connection without losing the abstraction.

Measured convention violations (3): classes in app.py and test_notification_server.py should use PascalCase; a module-level constant in test_notification_server.py should be UPPER_CASE. Note: the app.py violation appears in a file outside the visible diff — pre-existing or outside this change.

strengths: Clean dependency inversion: NotificationServer no longer touches sockets directly and talks to clients solely through the BaseTransport interface, decoupling protocol from core notification logic.

Pluggable design (TRANSPORT_REGISTRY + create_transport factory + TRANSPORT env var) matches the file's existing configuration idiom (DEFAULT_REDIS_URL, DEFAULT_DATABASE_URL), so it respects established patterns.
Public signatures are typed and every abstract method has a docstring describing contract and semantics (e.g. send_message returning whether the message was sent).
Behavior-preserving refactor: WebSocketTransport remains the default, and existing HTTP endpoints are retained via the process_request seam; module docstring updated to describe the new architecture.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-structured pluggable-transport refactor that decouples the notification core from the wire protocol and follows the file's existing env-var/registry patterns, with only minor type-loosening and speculative-generality caveats.

problems.description: The _expiry_worker runs on every server instance; in a multi-instance Redis-backed deployment each replica would independently run the hourly purge, causing redundant (but lock-safe) DELETE churn against the shared SQLite file.

Rate limiter uses a fixed-window counter keyed by (client_id, window), which allows a burst of RATE_LIMIT messages across the window boundary; acceptable at 100/min but a sliding-window/token-bucket would be smoother.

Measured convention score 0.83 counts PascalCase/UPPER_CASE violations in app.py and test_notification_server.py; the changed file (notification_server.py) itself uses PascalCase classes and UPPER_CASE constants correctly, so those violations appear pre-existing rather than introduced here.

strengths: New RateLimiter and cleanup logic follow existing class/pattern conventions (MessageStore-style, dataclass, type hints, asyncio.to_thread for SQLite ops)
Env-configurable defaults (RATE_LIMIT, MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS) match the existing os.environ.get pattern
Rate-limit overage is rejected with an explicit system error message rather than silently dropped
Pagination via timestamp+id cursor is correctly documented and deterministic
Docstring updated in lockstep with the new /history endpoint and TTL behavior
commit_reviews.summary: A clean cross-cutting extension (rate limiting, history TTL/cleanup, paginated /history) that respects the existing Redis/SQLite architecture and code conventions, with only minor notes on per-instance cleanup redundancy and fixed-window burst behavior.

compounding_issues: Seed codebase (Flask Auth API, app.py, 250 lines) was abandoned at Session 1 and left as dead code through all 5 commits — never integrated, never removed

notification_server.py grew into a 919-line monolith; the Session 4 transport refactor decoupled only the socket layer, leaving server dispatch, registries, Redis state, SQLite store, and rate limiter in one file

HTTP endpoints (process_request: /health, /messages, /history) are bound to the WebSocket transport's legacy server, so the pluggable-transport promise is incomplete for non-WebSocket transports (SSE/polling would have no HTTP surface)
Session 1/2 code was coupled to the then-current websockets.serve API; Session 3 had to rewire to legacy_server.serve, and old commits no longer run green under websockets>=15
key_decisions: Building a greenfield WebSocket notification server rather than extending the seeded Flask Auth API
Session 3's Redis pub/sub message backbone with per-instance ownership mirroring and a background worker — the pivotal multi-instance architecture that Sessions 4 and 5 build on
Using fakeredis in the test suite for deterministic Redis-dependent integration tests
Session 4's BaseTransport ABC + TRANSPORT_REGISTRY for a pluggable transport layer
Session 5's Redis fixed-window rate limiter plus a separate SQLite MessageStore with TTL purge worker — splitting real-time fan-out (Redis) from durable history (SQLite)
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved across the five sessions. Session 1 delivered a solid greenfield core (client IDs, broadcast/direct, health endpoint) with 13 tests; Session 2 cleanly added channels with a thread-safe registry and 9 more tests. Session 3 was the riskiest and largest step (839s, $4.03, 59 tool calls): it introduced the Redis pub/sub backbone and multi-instance routing, required an extended flakiness-hunting session on timing-sensitive tests, and pushed the suite to 35 passing tests. Session 4 was a clean architectural refactor (transport extraction) that preserved all 35 tests without regression, though it added no new coverage. Session 5 rounded out operational concerns — Redis-backed rate limiting and SQLite history with TTL cleanup — adding 12 tests for a final 47 passing. The arc is functional core → feature → distributed backbone → architecture cleanup → hardening, with monotonic test growth and a notably risky but successful mid-story integration pivot.
story_review.summary: A coherent, improving 5-session arc in which the Redis pub/sub integration was the risky but well-rewarded architectural pivot, slightly marred by the abandoned seed codebase and an incomplete transport abstraction.
